H1.text: A knife sharpener pedals to keep his stone spinning. A child pulls a string to spin a top.

H2.text: Each one gives a push, and the push turns into spin.

H3.text: Aarav watches a potter. She kicks the heavy wheel a few times, and it keeps turning for a long time.

H4.text: Each kick is a push at the rim. Where does the work of that kick go? And how much spin does it buy?

H5.text: To answer that, we need the dynamics of rotation.

P1.text: Push a cart, and three things matter: force, mass and acceleration.

P2.text: A turning wheel has a partner for each. Torque does the job of force.

P3.text: Moment of inertia does the job of mass: how hard the body is to spin.

P4.text: Angular acceleration does the job of acceleration: how fast the spin grows.

S1.text: Our motion notebook. A heavy wheel on a fixed axle. Its moment of inertia is four kilogram metre squared.

S2.text: The foot pushes the rim with twenty newtons, half a metre from the axle. Torque: twenty times half, ten newton metres.

S3.text: Watch it spin up. Alpha is torque over I. Ten over four. Two point five radians per second squared.

S4.text: After two seconds, the push stops. The wheel has turned five radians, and spins at five radians per second.

S5.text: The push is gone. Will the wheel slow down, or keep its spin? Ignore friction. Pause and decide.

S6.text: It keeps its spin! No torque, no angular acceleration. It stays at five radians per second.

S7.text: Slow-mo replay. Freeze in the middle of the push.

S8.text: In a tiny turn, d theta, the rim moves a small arc, r times d theta.

S9.text: The force acts along that arc. So the work is F r d theta. That is torque times d theta.

S10.text: On the graph, energy grows in a straight line with angle. The slope is the torque, ten joules per radian.

S11.text: Fifty joules of work went in. The wheel now holds exactly fifty joules of spin energy.

R1.text: But why does a spinning wheel have kinetic energy? Link by link.

R2.text: Every bit of the wheel moves in a circle. A bit at distance r moves at r omega.

R3.text: Its energy is one half m v squared, so one half m r squared omega squared.

R4.text: Add all the bits. The sum of m r squared is I. So the spin energy is one half I omega squared.

D1.text: Now the rules, one step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. Work in a tiny turn. d W equals F r d theta, which is tau d theta.

D3.text: Step two. For a steady torque, add up the tiny turns. W equals tau theta.

D4.text: Step three. Work per second is power. P equals tau omega.

D5.text: Step four. This power feeds the spin energy. Tau omega equals I omega alpha.

D6.text: Step five. Cancel omega. Tau equals I alpha. Newton's second law, for turning.

T1.text: Remember this. A torque does work as it turns, and that work becomes spin energy.

K1.text: Side by side. The same torque, ten newton metres, over the same five radians.

K2.text: A light wheel, with I equal to one. And a heavy wheel, with I equal to four.

K3.text: Now you try. Which wheel ends up with more spin energy? Pause and decide.

K4.text: The same! Both get fifty joules: the work, tau theta, is the same. The light wheel just spins faster.

W2.text: A motor spins a grinding wheel, I equal to zero point five, from rest to twenty radians per second in four seconds. Find torque, work and average power.

W3.text: Angular acceleration is twenty over four. Five radians per second squared.

W4.text: Torque is I alpha. Zero point five times five. Two point five newton metres.

W5.text: Work equals the spin energy gained. One half, times zero point five, times twenty squared. One hundred joules.

W6.text: Average power: one hundred over four. Twenty five watts.

X2.text: Many students put omega in r p m straight into one half I omega squared.

X3.text: But omega must be in radians per second. One hundred and twenty r p m is one hundred and twenty times two pi over sixty: four pi.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In torque and work, power, and flywheel energy questions.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A flywheel with I equal to two kilogram metre squared spins at six hundred r p m. A steady brake stops it in ten revolutions. Find the braking torque. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. Twenty pi newton metres.

A2.text: Omega: six hundred times two pi over sixty. Twenty pi radians per second.

A3.text: Spin energy: one half times two times twenty pi squared. Four hundred pi squared joules.

A4.text: Ten revolutions is twenty pi radians. Torque times twenty pi equals four hundred pi squared. So torque is twenty pi newton metres.

Y2.text: One. Why does the wheel keep spinning after the push stops?

Y3.text: Two. Why do a light and a heavy wheel get the same spin energy from the same push?

Y4.text: Three. Why must omega be in radians per second in one half I omega squared?

N1.text: Next time: spin on a chair and pull your arms in. Nobody pushes you, yet you speed up. How? Conservation of angular momentum.
